text.p: The Turkish lira closed weaker at 90,170 to the dollar on Thursday after 90,110 on Wednesday as banks' dollar demand continued despite a persistent cash squeeze.
Bankers said expectations of higher inflation in the last quarter were fuelling demand for the U.S. currency.
"Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's second ressource package did not affect the currency market," said one dealer.
Erbakan presented his government's second revenue-raising package aiming to earn another $10 billion after the first package disclosed on July 31.

The second package aims to mobilise 11 categories of resources including sale of excess property owned by troubled social security institutions, declaration of unregistered precious metal stocks and a new witholding tax on Treasury bills and bonds to be issued with a 1997 maturity.
Currency and stock markets were unmoved by the package instead, awaiting implementation of the package after an uninspiring first package.
The central bank set its dollar rate for banks' compulsory monthly hard currency transfers at 89,900 lira, up from 89,850 at Wednesday's close.
Bankers said cash demand remained strong as banks repaid the central bank 42.8 trillion lira o/n money borrowed at 75 percent on Wednesday.
Central bank injected a total of 38.75 trillion lira to the market to relieve the liquidity shortage.
It funded 8.75 trillion lira by buying seven-day repos from banks at an average annual rate of 73.83 percent on the open market.
The bank also funded 30 trillion lira overnight cash at 75 percent on the interbank. Overnight rates also traded at 74.75 percent.
In the t-bill market, yields ended lower in reaction to the new resource package. The yields had firmed by one point at the opening on tight liquidity.
Erbakan said a 10 percent withholding tax would be introduced on interest income from Treasury bills and bonds to be issued with a 1997 maturity, but the tax would not be retroactive.
"Yields dropped by one-to-two points from opening levels on buying after Erbakan said the withholding tax would not be charged on papers that are issued before the tax takes effect," said one banker.
The tax will go into effect after a related government decree is published in the official gazette.
The yield on the most active March 26, 1997 paper, dropped to 126.78 percent average from 126.87 percent Wednesday's average.
The second most heavily traded December 25 paper eased to 112.13 percent from Wednesday's 112.25 percent average.
